posts.title: Welcome to the Purple Room
posts.excerpt: How one velvet leaf turned into a climate-controlled atelier of rare anthurium in the heart of Saigon.
posts.body:
It started with a single **Carlablackiae** leaf on a windowsill.

What began as an obsession is now a climate-controlled room in Saigon, held at a steady 26°C and 70–85% humidity, where the rarest aroids are raised like living jewellery.

This journal is the workshop diary: grow notes, new unfurls, restock announcements and the quiet stories behind each specimen. No hype, no shortcuts — just velvet, veins and patience.

Welcome to the veinclusive purple selection.

posts.title: The Anatomy of Velvet
posts.excerpt: Why do some anthurium leaves look like cut velvet? The answer is structure, not pigment.
posts.body:
Why do some anthurium leaves look like cut velvet?

The effect is structural, not pigment. Tiny cone-shaped cells on the leaf surface scatter light in every direction, so the leaf drinks shine instead of reflecting it. Add pale, sunken veins and you get the quilted, three-dimensional look collectors chase.

### What velvet needs

- **Soft, even light.** Harsh sun flattens the nap and bleaches veins. Bright indirect is plenty.
- **Stable humidity.** Velvet forms as the leaf hardens off; swings give thin, matte foliage.
- **Airflow.** Gentle movement keeps those cells clean and prevents fungal spotting.

Get a leaf's *first two weeks* right and the velvet is set for life.

posts.title: How to Read a Rare Anthurium
posts.excerpt: Before you buy, learn to read a leaf. Three things separate a good specimen from a great one.
posts.body:
Before you buy, learn to read a leaf. Three things separate a good specimen from a great one.

### Vein
Look for high contrast and even spacing. Silver veins should feel *drawn on*, not muddy, and run symmetrically from the midrib.

### Velvet
Tilt the leaf to the light. True velvet shifts from near-black to deep green as the angle changes. A flat, glossy sheen is a younger or lower-grade leaf.

### Form
The best hearts are wide, deeply lobed and held flat. Cupping and narrow sinuses usually mean stress or unstable genetics.

A fair price follows the leaf, not the label. Learn the leaf first.

posts.title: The Saigon Humidity Playbook
posts.excerpt: Tropical city, dry apartment. How to hold 70–85% humidity when the air-con is fighting you.
posts.body:
Tropical city, dry apartment — the classic Saigon paradox. Air-conditioning can drop a room to 45% RH in minutes, and rare aroids hate it.

Here is the playbook that keeps the Purple room stable:

- **Cluster your plants.** Grouped foliage creates its own humid microclimate.
- **One good hygrometer per zone.** You manage what you measure.
- **Ultrasonic humidifier on a timer,** not a mister. Consistency beats intensity.
- **Airflow always.** A small clip fan on low prevents the stagnant, fungal air that high humidity invites.

Target 70–85% RH and, crucially, *keep it there.* Plants forgive a lower number far more easily than a swinging one.

posts.title: Caring for Carlablackiae
posts.excerpt: Velvet, bullate and notoriously fussy — the exact envelope that keeps Carla pushing perfect hearts.
posts.body:
Carlablackiae rewards consistency and punishes impatience.

### The envelope

- **Light:** bright indirect, roughly 120 µmol PAR, ~12h
- **Humidity:** 70–85% RH with gentle airflow
- **Medium:** chunky, airy aroid mix — never wet feet
- **Temp:** steady 24–26°C

The most common mistake is chasing fast growth with heavy feeding and strong light. Carla doesn't work that way. Slow, stable conditions are what give you the quilted velvet and silver veining people wait a decade to see.

When a new leaf pushes, resist the urge to move or repot. Let it harden in place.

posts.title: The New-Leaf Ritual
posts.excerpt: Every new arrival at Purple goes through the same quiet two-week ritual before it joins the room.
posts.body:
Every new arrival at Purple goes through the same quiet ritual before it joins the collection.

**Day 0 — Isolation.** New plants sit apart for two weeks. Pests and disease travel on the healthiest-looking leaves.

**Day 1 — Read and photograph.** We log the leaf: vein, velvet, form, any damage. It becomes the baseline for every future unfurl.

**Week 1 — Match the envelope.** Slowly bring humidity and light to room standard. No repotting, no feeding — just observation.

**Week 2 — Integrate.** If the newest leaf hardens off clean, the plant joins the room.

It is slower than most people expect. That is the point. Rare plants reward the patient keeper.
